item.question: Show that the mean of 10, 10, 11 and 17 balances the distances, and that 13 does not.
steps: Left of 12: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. Right of 12: 17 − 12 = 5. They are equal.
Try 13. Left of 13: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. Right of 13: 17 − 13 = 4. Not equal.
Try 11. Left of 11: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Right of 11: 6 + 0 = 6. Not equal.
item.answer: Only 12 balances the distances; 13 and 11 do not
item.text:
Worked example: Show that the mean of 10, 10, 11 and 17 balances the distances, and that 13 does not.
1. The mean is (10 + 10 + 11 + 17) ÷ 4 = 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
2. Left of 12: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. Right of 12: 17 − 12 = 5. They are equal.
3. Try 13. Left of 13: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. Right of 13: 17 − 13 = 4. Not equal.
4. Try 11. Left of 11: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Right of 11: 6 + 0 = 6. Not equal.
Answer: Only 12 balances the distances; 13 and 11 do not

item.question: Use algebra to show what happens to the mean when 2 is subtracted from every one of n values whose mean is a.
steps_tex: The values are $x1$, $x2$, … $xn$, and $(x1 + x2 + \ldots + xn) \div n = a$.
The new sum is $(x1 - 2) + (x2 - 2) + \ldots + (xn - 2) = x1 + x2 + \ldots + xn - 2n$.
Dividing by $n$ gives $a - 2$.

item.question: Find the mean of the following data and share your observations: (i) The first 50 natural numbers. (ii) The first 50 odd numbers. (iii) The first 50 multiples of 4.
steps_tex: (i): The sum is $50 \times 51 \div 2 = 1275$, so the mean is $1275 \div 50 = 25.5$.
(ii): The first $50$ odd numbers add to $50 \times 50 = 2500$, so the mean is $2500 \div 50 = 50$.
(iii): These are $4$ times the natural numbers, so the mean is $4 \times 25.5 = 102$.
Observation: for evenly spaced values the mean is the average of the first and the last value.

item.text:
$1$. The nine known weights add to $42 + 40 + 39 + 33 + 48 + 38 + 42 + 35 + 32 = 349$.
$2$. Let the missing weight be $w$. Then $(349 + w) \div 10 = 39.2$.
$3$. $349 + w = 39.2 \times 10 = 392$.
$4$. $w = 392 - 349 = 43$.
